title: David-Horodok welcomes the Red Army, then lives under repression and occupation
summary: The change from Polish rule to Soviet power and then German occupation overturned civic life and ushered in arrests and persecution.
editorialContent:
## A town caught between armies

In September 1939, David-Horodok was a Jewish town in eastern Poland, on the Horyn River. Germany had invaded Poland on September 1; as war approached, townspeople listened anxiously for news and worried about what might happen when German forces reached them. The memorial book recalls that Jewish residents hoped the Soviet advance would spare them from Nazi rule and from the antisemitic Polish government they had experienced. Their relief was real, but the choice before them was not between safety and danger: it was between authorities whose consequences they could not yet know. [The memorial book’s account of David-Horodok](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_bcbe8f6f5fb9a4059354cafb)

The [Red Army’s entry into David-Horodok](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_d018a1c641f62042c86f8001) followed the Polish withdrawal. The memorial book places the arrival on September 19, 1939, after Polish forces crossed the Horyn and destroyed the bridge; it describes a brief exchange of fire before Soviet soldiers crossed by pontoon. A second account in the book gives the Red Army’s entry as 6 a.m. that day. The accounts differ in emphasis and detail, so the precise sequence at the river should be read as remembered testimony rather than as a single independently verified minute-by-minute chronology. [A firefighter’s account in the memorial book, JewishGen’s translation](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_a7a45f36af6961a2897defe5)

Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos identifies Dawidgródek—another form of the town’s name—as a prewar town in Poland’s Polesie district, and describes its Jewish community as numbering about 3,000 between the wars. Its account independently places the town in the wartime geography later shaped by German occupation. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224&utm_source=openai))

## The welcome—and what followed it

The memorial book describes a public welcome after the fighting ended: Jewish and non-Jewish residents came into the streets, smiling and greeting the Soviet troops. [The celebration of the Red Army’s arrival](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_a7a45f36af6961a2897defe5) was led, in the book’s telling, by a small group of Jewish Communists and joined by other townspeople. Residents spoke with the soldiers about Polish rule and were encouraged by their accessibility and promises that Jews would no longer face the same troubles. The book remembers September 19 as a day of happiness and hope.

That welcome did not mean that Soviet rule left communal life untouched. The memorial book recalls that authorities prohibited Hebrew instruction, changing what children could learn at school. In one witness’s recollection, teacher Barentshuk struggled to tell pupils they would now study in Yiddish rather than Hebrew. The restriction threatened more than a curriculum: it struck at a language and educational tradition bound up with communal identity and hopes of emigration. [Barentshuk, the teacher named in the account](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_3cd0b3d6a10d6e71964c50a0)

The book also remembers residents who hoped to leave for the Land of Israel, and describes the new regime as narrowing those possibilities. That tension is important: the arrival was celebrated because it seemed to avert an immediate danger, while the Soviet authorities soon constrained institutions and choices the community valued. A wider historical account likewise states that the town came under Soviet control after the 1939 invasion of Poland and remained so until 1941. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davyd-Haradok?utm_source=openai))

## Arrests and the prison in Pinsk

In February 1941, Soviet repression became personal and frightening. The memorial book records that ten activists were arrested during the night of February 10–11. [The arrest of ten activists](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_a19e6f666e975c24f9e7299e) appears alongside another account of [arrests in the town on February 11](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_7059a3a853babd802d7e754c). Together, the records point to a nighttime roundup associated with political suspicion, but they do not establish that every detainee had the same affiliation or that the surviving accounts preserve a complete list.

Among the named detainees were Shmuel Zezik and Kopel Moravchik; the witness’s account connects their arrest to the political character of the imprisonment. Kopel Moravchik is also remembered as having later immigrated to Israel, though the supplied account does not establish his full family history or the details of his release. [Kopel Moravchik](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_2d04e4e0140e605f38164369) Arrests and interrogation did not end in town: detainees were transferred to [Pinsk’s central prison](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_314da5c9a05391fc43662b46). The move from the local streets to a regional prison shows how state power reached into the community and removed people from their families and neighbors.

The memorial book names people from several strands of David-Horodok’s communal and political life, but the records supplied here do not give enough information to reconstruct their family relationships or the circumstances of every person’s fate. Shmuel Tschtschik, for example, is remembered as a party leader who helped reorganize branch activity; that does not, by itself, establish that he was among the February detainees. [Shmuel Tschtschik](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_936d206e1ae600ad0d33ca9d) Likewise, Aharon Moravchik is named in connection with earlier political organization, but the supplied record does not establish a family relationship to Kopel. [Aharon Moravchik](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_450655fb29af7fe167d8a78d)

## German occupation ends the Soviet interlude

When Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, Soviet rule in David-Horodok was nearing its end. The memorial book says the Bolsheviks left in early July and German forces entered soon afterward. Its event record gives the occupation as July 1941; a separate chapter in the translated memorial book gives July 5, while Yad Vashem’s encyclopedia states that the Soviets withdrew on July 5. A Wikipedia town history gives German occupation as beginning July 7. These sources agree on the early-July transition but differ on the date of German entry; it would be misleading to turn them into a single precise date. [The German occupation of David-Horodok](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_b44aaba146a1460fdd8ee6f3)

The change of power was not a simple handover from one army to another. The memorial book recounts that, before German troops arrived, a local delegation went to the German authorities in Pinsk to urge their advance. This is the book’s account of local collaboration, not independent proof of the motives or conduct of every Christian resident. Yad Vashem’s town entry provides independent context for the German occupation and the destruction that followed, while the town history on Wikipedia also places the occupation in July 1941. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224&utm_source=openai))

The sequence remembered here—hope at the Red Army’s arrival, restrictions under Soviet rule, arrests and imprisonment, then German occupation—does not make the February arrests a direct cause of the Holocaust. It does show how rapidly the community’s security and autonomy narrowed. Under Soviet rule, activists could be seized and taken away; under German rule, the Jewish community faced a different and far more lethal persecution. The memorial book’s later chapters and independent records describe the town’s destruction, but this account stops at the transition into occupation rather than folding that later history into an event that began in 1939.
